overview.historicalContext: This problem belongs to Euclidean Ramsey theory, a field initiated by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus in the 1970s. The classical Ramsey theorem guarantees monochromatic cliques in edge-colored complete graphs; Euclidean Ramsey theory asks which geometric configurations must appear monochromatically in finite colorings of $\mathbb{R}^d$. Erdős posed Problem #173 [Er75f, Er83c] asking whether all but at most one triangle shape must have a monochromatic congruent copy in any 2-coloring of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Shader's 1976 breakthrough [Sh76] proved all right triangles are Ramsey using geometric constructions that exploit orthogonal reflections. The equilateral triangle is the natural candidate exception: a simple strip coloring demonstrates that specific equilateral triangles cannot be placed monochromatically. Kříž (1991) later developed permutation group methods for Euclidean Ramsey problems, and Frankl–Rödl (1990) established deep connections to partition regularity. The problem remains open and is central to the field.
overview.problemStatement:
**Problem Statement (OPEN)**

In any 2-coloring of $\mathbb{R}^2$, for all but at most one triangle $T$ (up to congruence), there is a monochromatic congruent copy of $T$.

**Known Results:**
- All right triangles are Ramsey (Shader 1976)
- The equilateral triangle is the candidate exception

**Counterexample Idea:**
Color $\mathbb{R}^2$ with alternating horizontal strips. An equilateral triangle of the right height cannot be placed monochromatically.
overview.text: In any 2-coloring of R^2, all but at most one triangle T has a monochromatic congruent copy. Shader proved this for all right triangles. The equilateral triangle is the candidate exception.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization builds up from basic Euclidean geometry: plane colorings ($\mathbb{R}^2 \to \text{Bool}$), triangle congruence via SSS (side-length permutations), and the Ramsey property. Triangle types (equilateral, right, isosceles) are defined. Shader's theorem is axiomatized and applied to the 3-4-5 triangle. The strip coloring construction demonstrates equilateral triangles are problematic. Similarity invariance shows the Ramsey property depends only on shape. The summary packages all results with the open conjecture.
keyInsights: The Ramsey property for triangles in $\mathbb{R}^2$ depends only on shape (similarity class), not size, because the plane admits arbitrary scaling
Shader's proof for right triangles exploits the orthogonal structure of right angles — reflections across axis-parallel lines preserve the strip coloring, enabling a pigeonhole argument
The strip coloring $\chi(x,y) = \lfloor y/h \rfloor \bmod 2$ is the key counterexample: equilateral triangles of height $h$ necessarily straddle a color boundary
The 'at most one exception' bound is tight: the strip coloring proves $\exists T$ equilateral with $\neg\text{IsRamseyTriangle}(T)$
The problem connects graph Ramsey theory (monochromatic cliques) to geometric Ramsey theory (monochromatic congruent copies), requiring fundamentally different techniques for the continuous setting

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #173 conjectures that in any 2-coloring of $\mathbb{R}^2$, all but at most one triangle shape has a monochromatic congruent copy. Shader (1976) proved this for all right triangles. The equilateral triangle is the candidate exception, as shown by the strip coloring counterexample. The formalization captures all known results, the counterexample construction, similarity invariance, and the open conjecture.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: A resolution would advance Euclidean Ramsey theory significantly.

Understanding which geometric configurations are 'unavoidable' under colorings connects to the chromatic number of the plane, Hales–Jewett-type results in geometry, and the broader program of classifying Ramsey configurations in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Shader's technique for right triangles does not extend to obtuse or acute triangles, suggesting new geometric or algebraic methods are needed.
openQuestions: Is the equilateral triangle the only non-Ramsey triangle shape in 2-colored $\mathbb{R}^2$?
Which triangles are Ramsey beyond right triangles? (Are all obtuse triangles Ramsey?)
What happens with $k$-colorings for $k > 2$? How many exceptions can there be?
Which configurations beyond triangles are Ramsey in $\mathbb{R}^2$? (Rectangles, parallelograms, etc.)
Do the results extend to higher dimensions $\mathbb{R}^d$?
